title: Gochujang: What It Is, How Spicy It Is, and How to Use It

seo.title: Gochujang: What It Is, How Spicy, and How to Use It
seo.meta_description: Gochujang is a Korean fermented paste made from red chile, grain, soybean, and salt. It combines heat, sweetness, salt, and umami, and its intensity varies widely by product.
seo.search_intent: Understand what gochujang is, how fermentation shapes its flavor, why it tastes sweet and umami as well as spicy, and how to use the paste in cooking.

excerpt: Gochujang is a thick Korean fermented paste traditionally made from red chile, glutinous rice or another grain, fermented soybean, and salt. It is not only hot: fermentation and grain contribute sweetness and umami, while chile intensity changes substantially among products.
content_html:
Gochujang is a thick Korean fermented paste combining red chile, grain, fermented soybean, and salt. Its flavor is not simply hot: it brings sweetness, saltiness, umami, and fermentation aromas, so one spoonful changes more in a dish than a thin chile sauce does.

Korea's agriculture ministry also emphasizes that gochujang has its own Codex standard and is recognized as a distinct fermented food rather than generic chili sauce.

What is traditionally in gochujang?

The Korean Food Promotion Institute describes a base of red pepper powder, glutinous-rice paste, meju powder from fermented soybean, and salt. Depending on region and producer, barley, wheat, brown rice, syrups, or other ingredients can appear.

Modern commercial products may use added sweeteners to adjust flavor and texture, so two tubs carrying the same product name can have noticeably different formulas.

Fermentation changes the flavor

Microorganisms associated with the fermented ingredients transform carbohydrates and proteins during maturation. Gochujang studies document changes in acidity, reducing sugars, and amino-type nitrogen as fermentation progresses.

Those amino compounds and fermentation products help create savory depth and aromas that an immediate mixture of chile, sugar, and salt cannot duplicate.

How spicy is gochujang?

There is no single heat level. Chile variety and amount, sweetness, salt, and fermentation all affect perception. Some retail gochujang is formulated to be mild, while other products are explicitly marketed as very hot.

Sugar and starch can soften the first impression of heat. A paste may taste sweet initially and become hotter several seconds later.

It is not used exactly like a thin hot sauce

Gochujang is concentrated and dense. It is often loosened with water, broth, sesame oil, vinegar, soy sauce, or other ingredients before becoming a pourable sauce.

A tablespoon can disappear into a stew or marinade, while the same amount eaten straight can dominate through salt, sweetness, fermentation, and chile heat all at once.

Classic and modern uses

Gochujang appears in bibimbap, tteokbokki, marinades, stews, meat sauces, and vegetable dishes. It can also be combined with doenjang, sesame oil, garlic, and other seasonings to create distinct condiments.

Outside Korea it now appears in mayonnaise, burgers, glazes, pasta, and roasted vegetables. These are modern applications but use the same sweet-hot-savory balance.

Why does it taste sweet if it is fermented chile paste?

Grain starch can be converted into sugars during processing, and many commercial formulas also contain syrup or added sugar. Sweetness is part of the condiment's characteristic balance.

When comparing brands, check ingredients and the nutrition panel rather than assuming they contain identical sugar or sodium levels.

How should an opened tub be stored?

Follow the manufacturer's label. Commercial products commonly recommend refrigeration after opening to maintain quality and reduce unwanted changes. Use clean utensils and reseal the container well.

Mild darkening or surface drying can be quality changes, while mold, clearly abnormal odor, or visible contamination are reasons to discard the product.

Why has gochujang become so international?

Codex adopted a worldwide standard specifically for gochujang in 2020, preserving its Korean name. Korean sauce exports have continued growing alongside broader international interest in Korean food.

The practical rule: think of gochujang as a concentrated fermented paste of chile, grain, and soybean rather than interchangeable hot sauce. Start with a small amount, dilute or mix it, and adjust for the specific product.

The practical value comes from understanding the mechanism before changing ingredients. Flavor, fermentation, and gelation depend on concentration, temperature, and the food matrix, so a substitution or amount that works in one recipe can behave differently in another.

faq.question: What is gochujang?
faq.answer: It is a Korean fermented paste made with red chile, grain, fermented soybean, and salt.

faq.question: How spicy is gochujang?
faq.answer: It varies by product from fairly mild to very hot, and sweetness changes how the heat is perceived.

faq.question: How do you use it?
faq.answer: Mix it into stews, marinades, and sauces or dilute it with other ingredients; it is concentrated and not normally used like a thin hot sauce.
